cells.tense: You are here at the page, choosing the direction instead of bracing against it.
cells.act: bear the next hour of it without deciding anything
cells.ask: Take one load you're carrying and give it a plain hour. Don't fix it. Don't decide about it. Stay in the hour and carry it as it actually weighs.
cells.core:
You can hold a direction with the whole shape still visible to you — pick it and see where it sits in the bigger picture at the same time. That picking comes out of clarity, not pressure. Because you can carry a load without forcing it, the load doesn't run your hands into a grip. A shape you're holding and a shape you're clenching look alike from outside; one of them can still move.

So when something heavy lands in your hands, stay with it without closing around it. Keep it the size it really is rather than trimming it down to something easier. Bear an ordinary hour of it and decide nothing about it. The old move turns weight into a verdict; you can let it stay weight a little past that. The grip is what tells you it's holding you; staying is something you pick.
cells.sheetLine: You can hold a direction without turning it into a grip.
cells.verb: choosing a direction and holding it
cells.place: seeing the whole thing from inside it

cells.tense: You will be forcing this direction through before it has had room to take shape.
cells.act: see the whole pattern you are standing inside
cells.ask: Take what you're driving and draw the whole set-up around it. Map the arrangement as it stands right now, with yourself on the page. Decide nothing after.
cells.core:
The last thing that started moving, you were already in front of it, arranging its next three steps. You can drive a direction forward so early that no one else has room to arrive at it, yourself included. What you'd call leading reads, from where others stand, like getting there first.

What keeps a direction from hardening into a grip is seeing the whole arrangement you're pushing, not pushing harder. Not the next move — the layout, with you marked on it. Sketch it and look at what you're standing inside. This adds no speed. It might cost some, and the thing you're forcing will still be there when you stop to see it. Nothing needs handling until you know how big it is.

cells.tense: You stopped at a door that already closed, and you are still standing at it.
cells.act: do one thing today the way only you do it, and do not explain it
cells.ask: One act today, done in your own particular way. No accounting for it to anybody afterward. Do it and stop there.
cells.core:
Direction has gone quiet here. It isn't that you can't see what's off — you see it fine. It's that choosing feels like it belongs to a version of you that stopped being around. So the days fill in without your hand in them, and their shape is set by whatever is already moving.

Going back and shoving on that door won't bring direction back. Something closer will: do one act today in your own particular way, and don't account for it to anyone. Nothing about it has to prove anything. You are already someone who does things a certain way; this lets that show in one ordinary act. The effort doesn't go into the closed door. It goes into the thing you can still make.

cells.tense: The direction is being followed, and no one has stopped to ask whose it is.
cells.act: put your own name on what is already yours
cells.ask: Pick a direction you've been moving in as if it were settled. Mark it yours. Jot your name on the note, the folder, wherever you'll run into it.
cells.core:
You move with momentum, and the path under you was laid down far enough back that it feels like the terrain. The direction itself is real. The selecting part has gone on autopilot, and the days are shaped by the plan rather than by the one walking it.

What is already yours doesn't need building fresh. It needs signing. Take a direction you've been following as if it were just how it goes — the shape you've given this, the way you handle that — and put your own name on it where you'll run into it. Then notice how it sits once you stop carrying it unsigned. You have been the one choosing. The record simply had no initials on file.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the reader is 'keeping the whole arrangement from being seen' — the record only says they confuse habit for choice, not that they withhold recognition from anyone; the reader could reasonably say they've never hidden anything, they just kept choosing the same direction out of habit. The ask survives being wrong: putting your name on something already done is useful whether the direction was chosen or drifted. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is 'the pattern has a keeper who has never once written their name on it' — it's a nice line, and the person might read it as a character judgment rather than a description of a habit. I've written it as a habit of leaving the name off, not as concealment.
